name: PostgreSQL
summary: The open-source relational database that most new projects start on, extensible enough to grow into many niches.
intro: PostgreSQL is a client-server SQL database. A supervisor process called the postmaster listens for connections and starts one operating-system process for each client. Concurrency comes from MVCC: an `UPDATE` writes a new version of the row instead of overwriting it, so each query sees a consistent snapshot, and reads never block writes. The cost is that old row versions pile up until `VACUUM`, usually run by the autovacuum daemon, reclaims them.

What sets it apart is how much it lets you add. Extensions plug new data types, index types and functions into the server, so PostGIS adds geospatial queries, pgvector adds vector search and TimescaleDB adds time-series storage, all with the same SQL and transactions. Built in, it has `jsonb` documents with GIN indexes, full-text search, window functions and serializable transactions. A new major version ships about once a year and gets five years of fixes.
strengths: Strict, standards-minded SQL with ACID transactions up to serializable isolation
Extensions such as PostGIS, pgvector and TimescaleDB turn one database into many
`jsonb` with GIN indexes covers many document-store use cases
Permissive BSD-style licence, and every major cloud offers it as a managed service
limits: One process per connection: thousands of clients need a pooler such as PgBouncer
MVCC leaves dead rows behind; autovacuum must keep up, or tables bloat and transaction IDs near wraparound
Writes scale up on one primary; scaling them out needs sharding through extensions or other systems
Major-version upgrades need `pg_upgrade`, a dump and restore, or replication to a new server, not just new binaries

snippet.title: Relational columns and an indexed JSON document in one table
source: id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
CREATE INDEX orders_details_idx ON orders USING gin (details jsonb_path_ops);
-- the containment operator @> can use the GIN index
SELECT id, customer_id, details->>'carrier' AS carrier

story: By the mid-1980s, relational databases handled business records well, but engineering work such as CAD, geographic data and graphics needed things like polygons and lines that the systems couldn’t store efficiently. Michael Stonebraker had led the Ingres project at UC Berkeley, but its code had been “hacked up enough” that adding major new features was extremely difficult. So in 1986 he and Lawrence Rowe designed a successor, POSTGRES (“post-Ingres”), whose goals included letting users add their own data types, operators and access methods. Implementation began that year, funded by DARPA, the Army Research Office, the NSF and ESL, Inc.

Berkeley released versions 1 to 4.2 from 1989, all using the project’s own query language, PostQUEL. As the research wound down, students Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen swapped PostQUEL for SQL in 1994 and released the result as Postgres95. Volunteers outside Berkeley adopted the code, renamed it PostgreSQL in 1996 and released version 6.0 in January 1997. They have run it ever since as the PostgreSQL Global Development Group.

A permissive licence and an extensible core made it a common starting point for commercial databases and for extensions such as PostGIS. In 2010 Heroku made it the default database on its platform, which helped frameworks such as Ruby on Rails and Django recommend it too.

choices.choice: Users can add types, operators and index methods
choices.why: Engineering data could be faked with plain tables, but the 1986 design paper called the resulting performance unacceptable. Making the type system and access methods pluggable is why PostGIS, pgvector and TimescaleDB can exist as extensions.

The designers knew a single server process would perform better, but it meant writing what amounted to a special-purpose operating system. With a small team, they chose the simpler process-per-user model on Unix, which is why PostgreSQL still needs a pooler for thousands of clients.

choices.choice: Write new row versions instead of overwriting
choices.why: POSTGRES kept every record as a chain of versions stamped with transaction IDs, which simplified crash recovery and allowed “as of” queries. PostgreSQL later added a write-ahead log and dropped time travel, but kept the versions for MVCC, and with them the need for `VACUUM`.

timeline.text: POSTGRES project begins at UC Berkeley under Michael Stonebraker
Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen add SQL, creating Postgres95
Renamed PostgreSQL; version 6.0 follows in January 1997
9.0 adds built-in streaming replication and hot standby
